accepted_phrases: Determine charging and data behavior from the intersection of the exact phone, protocol, selected charger port, sharing state, and cable rather than from connector shape or one maximum-wattage label. The ULTRANET page claims up to 65 W from its USB-C port with one device and shared allocation with two devices, while its MacBook claim requires a separately sold E-Mark cable. The ALOGIC page claims USB-C port 1 at 100 W alone but 65 W when all outputs are active, USB-C port 2 at 18 W, and the USB-A pair sharing 17 W. The two USB-C cable pages claim different limits: one claims 100 W, 20 Gbit/s, an E-Marker, and conditional DisplayPort Alternate Mode video, while the other claims 60 W and USB 2.0 or 480 Mbit/s data. USB devices negotiate speed and power. The Galaxy S22 family has exact PPS and non-PPS profiles, and the Realme GT Neo5 advertised rate requires its proprietary bundle. These ceilings and profiles define possible intersections but do not guarantee that every combination reaches its fastest printed number.

Keep the owner reports as scoped troubleshooting observations. One iPhone 14 Pro Max author reports one percentage point in five minutes near 75 percent with both MagSafe and a Lightning cable connected to a 30 W USB-C brick, then seven percentage points in four minutes from 49 percent. This changes battery state and charging method, and the phone-side wired connector is Lightning. One iPhone XS Max author reports MFi-cable failures after back-glass repair while an official 20 W combination and wireless charging worked, then says compressed-air removal of small port debris fixed the problem. Repair timing and debris prevent protocol or charger attribution. A third thread contains one report of rapid Lightning pin failures and another careful user's report that official Apple cables had not failed. These individual Lightning experiences do not establish USB-C contact life, product reliability, or a population brand ranking. Product pages remain seller claims, and the S22 and Realme examples remain exact-model capability examples rather than explanations of those iPhone incidents.

USB began as a way to standardize peripheral connections and replace several older interfaces. Standard, Mini, and Micro connector forms preceded Type-C. USB-C is reversible and can carry several protocols and functions, many of which are optional according to the hardware; backward compatibility can reduce signaling rate, offered power, or other capabilities. The USB hardware page also separates power, data, and role behavior, including a standard USB-C cable specified for 60 W and at least USB 2.0 data. The seller snapshots illustrate the consequence: two cables with USB-C connectors claim 100 W and 20 Gbit/s versus 60 W and 480 Mbit/s. Connector convergence therefore simplifies physical connection without making protocol, power, data, video, or role capability identical.

Make only an evidence-bounded conditional shortlist. The two charger pages and two cable pages state useful port, sharing, power, data, e-marker, and alternate-mode conditions, but they are seller snapshots rather than independent tests. The iPhone threads reveal possible charge-state, debris, repair, connector, and handling variables, but they are individual Lightning or MagSafe experiences rather than USB-C reliability studies. The general USB pages explain optional functions and negotiation but do not certify a product. Because no source supplies a controlled family-device matrix or longitudinal reliability comparison, do not name one universally trusted brick or cable and do not promise the fastest mode for every combination. Keep only candidates whose documented port profiles and cable capabilities match each exact phone, and require direct combination testing before consolidating the drawer.

Build one row for each phone, brick, selected port, and cable combination. Record the exact phone model and connector, documented charging protocols and voltage-current profiles, PPS support, and any proprietary-bundle requirement. Record the exact charger model, selected port, that port's profiles, and its allocation with other ports occupied. Record cable endpoints, current or power rating, USB data generation, e-marker status when relevant, and video or alternate-mode limits. Test one combination at a time with the same starting battery range, temperature, phone activity, elapsed interval, and other-port occupancy. Log negotiated mode when observable, battery percentage change, measured power when suitable equipment is available, temperature, disconnects, data rate or video result when relevant, and the change after connecting a second device. A successful run supports only that exact combination and condition, so retain model-specific documentation and repeat suspect results.

Treat USB-C as a shared connector rather than a universal performance label. Explain its historical convergence and then separate connector, protocol, charger port and sharing state, phone-supported profile or proprietary bundle, cable power and data capability, and device state. Audit the ULTRANET and ALOGIC ports and both cable pages only as seller claims at their stated conditions. Keep the S22 PPS values and Realme GT Neo5 bundle requirement at exact model scope, and keep the iPhone reports as Lightning or MagSafe observations with battery-state, repair, debris, and handling confounders. Since the material has no controlled family-device matrix and no longitudinal reliability study, name no universally fastest or trusted product. Make a conditional shortlist from documented intersections, then complete the phone-by-brick-by-port-by-cable matrix and controlled tests before discarding the old equipment.
Use documented per-phone compatibility and controlled combination tests to make conditional charger and cable choices, while declining to name a universal fastest or trusted winner.
Treat the products only as conditional candidates, build the phone-by-brick-by-port-by-cable matrix, and do not claim one charger or cable is universally fastest or reliable.

The material documents different charger-port allocations, different cable power and data claims, USB negotiation, exact S22 profiles, one Realme GT Neo5 proprietary bundle, and several scoped iPhone incidents, but contains neither a controlled family-device compatibility matrix nor a longitudinal charger or cable reliability comparison.
A common USB-C connector reduces physical plug variation but leaves protocol, port, phone, cable, data, video, power, and state capabilities separate.
Seller specifications can define conditional candidates and community incidents can suggest troubleshooting variables, but neither is an independent performance or population reliability study.

A controlled test can verify one recorded phone, brick, port, cable, occupancy, battery-state, and temperature condition, but it cannot establish universal fastest-mode support or long-term reliability.
Any two devices, chargers, or cables with USB-C connectors support the same power, data speed, video modes, and protocols.
The 100 W 20 Gbit/s cable and the 60 W USB 2.0 cable are functionally identical because both have USB-C plugs.
The ULTRANET charger supplies 65 W independently to both connected devices at the same time.
Every ALOGIC port provides 100 W, including USB-C port 2 and both USB-A ports, even when all outputs are active.
The 100 W cable always provides 4K video even when the connected USB-C port does not support DisplayPort Alternate Mode.
The Anker 60 W USB 2.0 cable supports the same 20 Gbit/s data rate claimed by the other USB-C cable.
Every Galaxy S22 family model charges at 45 W without PPS.
The listed Galaxy S22 charging profiles apply unchanged to every Samsung Galaxy phone.
Every Oppo, Realme, and OnePlus phone requires the Realme GT Neo5 proprietary charger and cable and supports its advertised 240 W rate.
The iPhone 14 Pro Max report proves that the 30 W USB-C brick was defective because charging near 75 percent was slow.
The repaired iPhone XS Max report proves that generic power bricks and MFi cables are protocol-incompatible with that phone.
The Lightning pin anecdotes establish the lifetime and brand reliability of USB-C cable contacts.
The seller pages prove that one listed charger and cable pair is universally fastest and reliable for every family phone.
One successful charging test proves the same speed, compatibility, and long-term reliability across every phone, port, cable, battery state, temperature, and multiport load.

research_subgoals.description: Explain the historical convergence on USB-C while separating connector shape from optional power, data, video, protocol, and role capabilities.
Compare the exact charger-port and cable claims with USB negotiation and the model-specific S22 and Realme charging constraints.
Audit the iPhone charging, repair, debris, and Lightning-pin reports without converting them or the seller pages into protocol causes or reliability rankings.
Construct a per-phone, per-brick, per-port, and per-cable compatibility and measurement matrix that respects port sharing, phone profiles, cable limits, and test state.
Make only conditional consolidation choices, state why no universal fastest or trusted winner is supported, and define what one controlled combination test can establish.

query_requirements.text: Trace how USB connections moved from older Standard, Mini, and Micro forms toward reversible USB-C, and explain why a common connector still leaves power, data, video, protocol, and device-role functions optional or different.

Compare the two charger listings port by port and the two USB-C cables by claimed power, data rate, e-marker, video condition, single-device ceiling, and multiport allocation; relate those claims to negotiation, the exact Galaxy S22 PPS profiles, and the Realme GT Neo5 bundle requirement.

Audit the owner reports in a compact table that keeps the phone model, phone-side connector or MagSafe method, battery state, repair history, debris, observed outcome, and remaining confounders separate; do not transfer Lightning experiences to USB-C durability or a brand reliability ranking.

Build a practical matrix with one row per phone, brick, selected port, cable, and other-port occupancy. Specify which documented profile and cable fields to record, how to control battery state and temperature, and what charging, data, video, disconnect, and multiport-change measurements to log.

Recommend only conditional charger and cable candidates whose documented capabilities intersect with each exact phone, say explicitly whether any universal fastest or trusted winner is supported, and distinguish what one controlled test can verify from the unanswered long-term reliability question.
